newsitem.title: THAILAND: Asian bank governors seen discussing dollar's rise.
newsitem.headline: Asian bank governors seen discussing dollar's rise.

text.p: The effect of a strong U.S. dollar on Asian currencies is expected to figure on the agenda of a meeting of 10 Asian central bank governors here later this week, officials said on Tuesday.
"The strength of the dollar and its impact on Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) currencies may be taken up," a Philippine central bank official said.
No specific agenda has been set for the annual meeting, but they expect the governors to exchange views on their respective country's monetary policies and current economic conditions.
The conference comes on the heels of last weekend's Group of Seven (G7) meeting of industrialised countries, which called for keeping the dollar stable after its strong rise over the past two years.
Some Asian curencies, particularly the Thai baht, have come under pressure from the dollar's recent surge.

The baht, which recently fell to a 6-1/2 year low against the dollar, has been under intermittent attack from currency speculators. The central bank is fighting back with high interest rates and costly offshore market intervention.
There also has been market speculation of an imminent baht devaluation against a backdrop of a sluggish Thai economy, a wide current account deficit and slowing export growth.

"There will be no special agenda for the meeting. It's just a regular meeting. The participating governors will exchange views on economic conditions in each country in the region. There will be no significant agreements in the meeting," said a spokeswoman for the host, the Bank of Thailand.

The central bank governors of Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Sri lanka, Nepal, Taiwan, Burma and South Korea will attend the 32nd SEACEN Governors Conference in Bangkok from February 13-16.
Observers from Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Fiji, Tonga and Papua New Guinea will also attend.
A special guest will be Germany's Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer, who has been invited to deliver an address on European economic and monetary union.
Most analysts do not expect the central bankers to come up with any kind of joint plan or a collective decision to resolve common currency or other economic woes.
Taiwan's central bank governor, Sheu Yuan-dong, was expected to brief others on his country's monetary policy.
Economists said Sheu likely would review Taiwan's progress in market liberalisation, its stable-to-loose monetary policy and the impact of the strong U.S. dollar.

"Governor Sheu will likely discuss the bank's decision to maintain a stable-to-loose monetary policy as the domestic economy has yet to show an ideal recovery," said Daniel Chen, chief economist for Chinatrust Commercial Bank.
Other analysts said the governors would also discuss the state of their respective economies and outlook for this year.
The governors could also review how various repurchase pacts among central banks in the region were working.

The central banks of Japan, Australia, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand have established bilateral repurchase agreements to provide each other with liquidity in times of currency crisis.

"We have yet to see these repo pacts in real action because the bottom line is that no country is really ready to help another fight speculation using valuable cash," said a senior dealer at a foreign bank in Thailand.
